subject: fabergeEgg
pitch:
Category: Object.
Subject: jewelled egg opening to reveal a tiny automaton.
Style: Fabergé enamel and gold.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through how to design a jewelled Fabergé-style egg with a hinged lid that opens to reveal a tiny automaton inside, considering realistic scale and joint structure for the hinge mechanism.

I'm planning the structure: a lathed gold pedestal with enamel bands and tripod feet holding the egg, then lower and upper egg shells lathed with custom guilloché enamel paint patterns using radial rays and wavy height lines, forming the hinged lid.

For the lid hinge, I'm working out the rotation math — hinging at the back rim about the X axis, computing how the lid's front point moves through rotation so it swings open and leans back convincingly, landing on roughly -100 degrees to show the interior.

Computing the lid center position relative to the hinge after rotation, I get it shifted up by about R and slightly back, so the lid stands roughly vertical behind the hinge with its rim forming a near-vertical disk and opening facing forward.

I should remember that geometry is built in closed position within the lid's bone hierarchy first, and the pose is applied afterward — anything built after the pose call would land in the posed orientation instead, so the sequence must be build all lid parts first, then call pose on the lid joint at the end.

Now I'm thinking through what sits inside the lower half — a tiny clockwork automaton standing on a small platform, maybe styled as a miniature brass figure with a round painted face and a wind-up key, in the spirit of Fabergé-style mechanical surprises.

I'm working out the proportions: egg roughly 12cm tall, the lower half cut around 55% up where the shell is near its widest, giving a cavity about 6.6cm deep, with the automaton figure around 5cm tall standing on a small platform so its head rises just above the rim.

I'm now defining the egg's parametric cross-section, scaling it up to about 16cm tall with an 11cm max diameter plus a 5cm stand, and writing the formula for how the radius varies with height to get that classic egg curve.

Still defining the lathe profile...

I'm checking proportions—the automaton figure stands too tall relative to the platform rim, so I'm considering raising the stage on a small gold coil spring under the floor, giving it a charming "pop-up surprise" effect while keeping the figure's scale believable inside the egg.

I'm now setting up the coordinate system: placing the egg's local axis origin at EGG_Y = 0.052 (where the stand cup meets the egg bottom), defining the lathe outline relative to that origin, and applying the same local frame to the lid so both share consistent y-coordinates for the hinge calculation.

For the lid shell itself, I'm tracing the outline from rim outer up to the top, then back down the inner wall to the rim, deduplicating the top points. I'm settling on around 16-20 segments for the egg's faceted low-poly look with sharp creases preserved at steep profile corners.

For the enamel treatment, I'm thinking a guilloché pattern in deep raspberry/ruby translucent enamel with gold banding at the rim and gold meridian ribs swept across the shell, accented with pearls and gemstones.

I'm writing the guilloché paint function now...

Still writing paint shader...

For the gold ribs, I'm thinking of sweeping thin meridian strips along the egg's curved surface using a path built from the egg profile function, attaching them to the lid or shell bone as needed, and placing just 4 ribs at diagonal angles (45°, 135°, 225°, 315°) so the front/back hinge and clasp area stays clear.

I'm also planning decorative medallion decals between the ribs — maybe a monogram at the front and painted ovals on the lower panels — but I need to figure out exact placement angles so they don't collide with the hinge knuckle I want mounted at the back.

For placing decals I'm positioning them on the shell surface using approximate normal directions based on angle, with the world up vector as default orientation, accounting for the lid's tilt when drawing its medallion.

I'm designing two Fabergé-style decal textures: a gold-ringed oval with beaded edge and ivory interior painted with blue forget-me-not flowers, and a second with a crown ornament, avoiding any real historical ciphers or dates.

For the finishing touches, I'll make the decal background transparent so it reads as a floating oval jewel-plaque, slightly raised off the shell surface. Around the medallion rim I'll add small squashed-sphere "gems" at 45° intervals with modest emissive glow to suggest cabochon jewels without overdoing the sparkle.

For materials, I'm leaning toward faceted icosahedron geometry for diamonds and squashed low-poly spheres for cabochon rubies, with flat unlit coloring for clarity. Gold trim will use a gilt metal paint with light polish and minimal tarnish, shared across parts to respect the single-material-per-paint-sheet rule.

For the stand design, I'm thinking of a Fabergé-style tiered gold pedestal, maybe swapping the simpler tripod-leg option with a tiered lathe base featuring an enamel band and a baluster stem leading up to an acanthus-leaf cup cradling the egg.

Checking the egg radius near the bottom to size the cup ring correctly, I calculate roughly 0.0315 at that height, so the cup should taper to match.

Now I'm sketching out leaves around the cup, curling outward and up toward the egg with flattened elliptical cross-sections, trying to figure out the best sweep approach for their orientation.

The leaf shape should taper to a point fine, so I'll move forward with this approach. I'm considering adding small bun feet beneath the base and a blue guilloché enamel band around the base using a lathe technique.

Now I'm planning the enamel ring as a separate thin lathe piece layered onto the base, and roughing out the full part inventory for the stand -- base lathe, enamel band, and a ring of pearls merged into a single geometry using mergeGeometries for efficiency, aiming for over 200 total parts across the whole piece.

For the egg itself, I'm figuring out how to handle the shell's interior lining without z-fighting -- making the outer shell a thick enameled lathe piece, then adding a separate thin lining lathe fitted just inside the cavity surface to represent the cream/ivory or gold interior finish.
